content.title: About
content.content: Soft shell crab is a crab that has recently molted, shedding its hard exoskeleton and leaving only a thin, edible shell. It has a delicate, slightly sweet flavor and a crisp texture that resembles other seafood.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soft shell crabs are harvested during the molting period when their shells are still soft.
In Japan, soft shell crab is a prized delicacy often served in sushi and tempura.
Crabs can molt several times a year, but only during molting are they suitable as soft shell.
The whole crab—including head, tail, and legs—is usually served.
When cooked properly, the meat stays moist and does not become dry.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Soft shell crab provides high‑quality marine protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many seafoods, it contains very little fat, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Source of omega‑3
items.content: It contains beneficial omega‑3 fatty acids that support heart and vascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The crab supplies B12, B6, and niacin, which are important for normal metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Crab is rich in zinc, selenium, and copper, minerals that aid immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to crab, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Although low in fat, crab contains cholesterol, so people with hypercholesterolemia should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Potential toxins
items.content: Crabs harvested from polluted waters can accumulate heavy metals and toxins; purchase only from reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soft shell crab is commonly deep‑fried, baked in a batter, or grilled. It can be served whole, split in half, or used in salads, sushi, and pasta dishes. Before cooking, rinse the crab under cold water and pat dry.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store soft shell crab in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C in an airtight container for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze it in a vacuum‑sealed bag for up to 3 months. Thaw frozen crab in the refrigerator before use.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato hash brown with cheese is made from fresh potatoes grated coarsely, mixed with shredded cheese, spices and a small amount of flour. The mixture is shaped into small patties and fried until golden and crisp. It is a hearty, flavorful snack popular in fast‑food and home cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hash brown originated in the United States in the early 20th century as a way to use leftover potatoes.
Adding cheese gives the patty a richer, umami flavor and a softer interior.
Traditionally hash browns are served with sour cream or ketchup.
In some regions they are called "potato pancakes" or "potato croquettes".
A vegetarian version without meat but with cheese fits most diets.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Fresh potatoes contain vitamin C, which helps strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Protein from cheese
items.content: Shredded cheese adds complete protein and calcium important for bone health.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Hash browns provide quick energy from carbohydrates.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Potato skin and a small amount of flour supply fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Frying in oil increases calories and saturated fat levels.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or dairy allergies.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Cheese is often salty, making the dish high in sodium, which may be unsuitable for hypertension.

items.title: Oil degradation at high heat
items.content: Overheating oil can create harmful compounds; it is recommended to fry at medium temperature.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot as a standalone snack, as a side to salads, or inside burgers. Sprinkle with fresh herbs, add sour cream, yogurt sauce, or a spicy dip to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked hash browns in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a single layer on a tray, then transfer to a freezer bag – they keep well for up to 2 months. Reheat in the oven to restore crispness.

rice-brown-with-carrots-dark-green-veget.title: Brown Rice with Carrots, Dark Green Vegetables and Tomato Sauce, Fat Added

content.title: About
content.content: This dish consists of brown rice, sautéed carrots, dark green vegetables (such as broccoli or spinach) and a tomato‑based sauce enriched with added fat (vegetable or butter). The combination of whole grains, vegetables and fat provides a balanced mix of carbohydrates, fiber, vitamins and healthy fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains the bran and germ, giving it more fiber and micronutrients than white rice.
Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant whose availability increases with cooking.
Dark green vegetables like broccoli, spinach and kale are among the richest sources of vitamin K and folate.
Adding a modest amount of fat enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) from the vegetables.
The dish can be easily adapted to various cuisines by changing spices and the type of sauce.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Brown rice and vegetables supply dietary fiber that supports regular digestion and a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Rice provides a steady release of energy, helping to maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Tomatoes, carrots and dark green vegetables are rich in vitamins A, C, K, as well as potassium and magnesium.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and carotenoids from carrots help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: The added fat improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins and adds satiety.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: The added fat increases the dish’s calorie content, so portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Fat allergies
items.content: Individuals allergic to certain vegetable oils or dairy fats should choose an appropriate fat source.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Some dark green vegetables (e.g., spinach) contain oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a main meal or side. It pairs well with a lean protein (chicken, fish, tofu) and can be topped with seeds (sesame, pumpkin) for extra crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat with a splash of water or broth to restore moisture.

content.title: About
content.content: Tortellini are small ring-shaped pasta filled with creamy cheese. This version contains no meat and is served with a light vinaigrette made from olive oil, vinegar, and fresh herbs. Tortellini cook quickly and their delicate flavor makes them popular in both cold and warm salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tortellini originate from Italy, where they were traditionally meat‑filled, but vegetarian versions became common in the 1920s.
The creamy cheese filling provides a smooth texture and a subtle tang that pairs well with vinaigrette.
The vinaigrette often includes balsamic vinegar, which highlights the cheese’s flavor.
Tortellini can be steamed, boiled in salted water, or baked in the oven with sauce.
They are frequently served in cold salads during summer because they cool quickly and hold their shape.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: The cheese filling supplies calcium, essential for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Durum wheat pasta and cheese provide both plant and dairy protein for tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Absence of meat makes the dish lower in saturated fat compared with traditional versions.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Durum wheat and cheese contain B1, B2, and B6, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants in vinaigrette
items.content: Olive oil and vinegar are rich in polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cheese may cause discomfort for people who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Tortellini made from wheat contain gluten, unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cheese and prepared vinaigrette can be salty; sodium‑sensitive individuals should watch portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: While less fatty, cheese and oil add calories; moderation is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve tortellini cold in a salad tossed with vinaigrette, or gently warm them. They pair well with leafy greens, cherry tomatoes, and nuts for extra crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry tortellini in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked pasta and vinaigrette should be refrigerated and consumed within 3 days.
